(CNN) -- An Ohio man who was suspended as the drum major of a band for giving President Obama a nod during last week's inaugural parade is calling it quits. John Coleman quit his band after it suspended him for nodding to President Obama last week. John Coleman resigned from the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums a week after the parade in Washington. Publicity about his suspension had gotten to be too much, he told CNN affiliate WEWS. "It's come to a point where I don't want embarrassment anymore between the pipe band and myself," Coleman, who is a firefighter, told WEWS on Tuesday. Coleman was seen during the nationally televised January 20 parade nodding toward the new president while marching with the band. A few steps later, he appeared to wave briefly. He told WEWS that as the band was marching past the grandstand where Obama was sitting, he made eye contact with the president. "Contact was made with our eyes both together and he smiled and waved at the band," he told the station. "And just as a gesture, I nodded my head. I gave him a slight wave and went on."  Watch parade and explanation » . Representatives from the group did not return calls from CNN. But bandleader Mike Engle told the Cleveland Plain Dealer that Coleman was suspended because he ignored military protocol. "We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade," Engle told the newspaper. "Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that." Coleman had been suspended from the band for six months. In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka said Coleman's resignation from the group "comes as a shock and surprise." The band has been inundated with phone calls, e-mails and messages on its Internet pages -- almost all of them critical -- since the story first broke on Monday, Rybka said. iReport.com: 'Pretty cool thing that he acknowledged the president' "It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public," Rybka said in the statement. "It has disheartened me more than you can imagine." Rybka said that he will be taking a leave of absence from the band because of the furor. "The 'afterglow' of participating in the inaugural parade is gone," he said.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — An Ohio man suspended from his role as drum major of a band after nodding to President Obama during last week’s inaugural parade has decided to resign.

John Coleman, a firefighter, left the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums one week after the parade in Washington. He told CNN affiliate WEWS that the publicity surrounding his suspension had become overwhelming.

“It’s come to a point where I don’t want embarrassment anymore between the pipe band and myself,” Coleman told WEWS on Tuesday.

Coleman was seen during the nationally televised January 20 parade nodding toward the newly inaugurated president while marching with the band. A few steps later, he appeared to give a brief wave.

He told WEWS that, as the band marched past the grandstand where Obama was seated, he made eye contact with the president.

“Contact was made with our eyes both together and he smiled and waved at the band,” Coleman told the station. “And just as a gesture, I nodded my head. I gave him a slight wave and went on.”

Watch parade and explanation »

Representatives from the group did not return calls from CNN. However, bandleader Mike Engle told *The Cleveland Plain Dealer* that Coleman was suspended because he had disregarded military protocol.

“We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade,” Engle told the newspaper. “Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that.”

Coleman had been suspended from the band for six months.

In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka said Coleman’s resignation from the group “comes as a shock and surprise.”

Rybka said the band has been inundated with phone calls, emails, and messages on its Internet pages—almost all of them critical—since the story first broke on Monday.

iReport.com: “Pretty cool thing that he acknowledged the president”

“It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public,” Rybka said in the statement. “It has disheartened me more than you can imagine.”

Rybka said he will be taking a leave of absence from the band because of the furor.

“The ‘afterglow’ of participating in the inaugural parade is gone,” he said.
outputs.L2:
An Ohio firefighter removed from his role as a band drum major after acknowledging President Barack Obama during the inaugural parade has decided to leave the group.

John Coleman resigned from the Cleveland Firefighters Memorial Pipes & Drums about a week after taking part in the Washington parade. He told CNN affiliate WEWS that the attention surrounding his suspension had become overwhelming.

“It’s come to a point where I don’t want embarrassment anymore between the pipe band and myself,” Coleman told WEWS on Tuesday.

During the nationally broadcast January 20 inaugural parade, Coleman was shown marching with the band when he nodded in Obama’s direction. Moments later, he appeared to make a short wave.

Coleman said the gesture happened as the band passed the reviewing stand where the newly inaugurated president was seated. According to Coleman, he and Obama briefly made eye contact.

“Contact was made with our eyes both together and he smiled and waved at the band,” Coleman told the station. “And just as a gesture, I nodded my head. I gave him a slight wave and went on.”

CNN said representatives of the band did not respond to its calls. However, bandleader Mike Engle told the Cleveland Plain Dealer that Coleman was disciplined because he failed to follow military parade protocol.

“We had gone over and over time and again with everyone in the band that this was a military parade,” Engle told the paper. “Protocol and proper decorum had to be followed at all times. Unfortunately, John chose to ignore that.”

Coleman had received a six-month suspension from the band.

In a written statement, band manager Ken Rybka said Coleman’s decision to resign “comes as a shock and surprise.”

Rybka said that after the story became public on Monday, the band was flooded with phone calls, emails, and online messages, nearly all of them negative.

“It is unfortunate that an internal band issue has raised so much discussion and ire from the general public,” Rybka said. “It has disheartened me more than you can imagine.”

Because of the backlash, Rybka said he also planned to take a leave of absence from the band.

“The ‘afterglow’ of participating in the inaugural parade is gone,” he said.
